title: Cut a release with a tag and notes

scenario.brief:
**The ticket.** `main` is ready to ship as **v1.5.0**. Your job: mark this exact point in history as a release, so anyone can come back to it, and write short notes saying what changed.

Two pieces:

1. A **tag** — a permanent name for this commit, like a bookmark: `v1.5.0`.
2. A **release** on GitHub — the tag plus human-readable notes, shown on the repo's Releases page.

**Your steps.** Make the tag, push it, then create the release on GitHub (or with the `gh` CLI) with a couple of lines of notes. When it's published, press **Check my work**.
scenario.whyItMatters: Tags and releases are how a team says "this exact code is version X." Support, rollbacks and changelogs all point at releases. Cutting one cleanly is a basic release-duty skill.

setup: Make sure you're on an up-to-date `main`.
Create an annotated tag for the release and push it to GitHub.
On GitHub, open **Releases → Draft a new release**, choose the `v1.5.0` tag, add a title and a couple of lines of notes, and publish. (Or use the `gh release create` command.)
Come back and press **Check my work**.
commands: gh release create v1.5.0 --title "Ledgerly 1.5.0" --notes "Invoice PDF export and tax rounding fix."

objectives.title: Create and push the v1.5.0 tag
hints: `git tag -a v1.5.0 -m "..."` makes an annotated tag on your current commit.
Tags aren't pushed by default — send it with `git push origin v1.5.0`.
Check on GitHub: the tag should appear under the repo's tags.

objectives.title: Publish a GitHub release for v1.5.0 with notes
hints: A release wraps the tag with notes. Releases → Draft a new release → pick v1.5.0.
Add a short title and a line or two of notes, then Publish.

debrief.summary: You tagged an exact commit as v1.5.0 and published a release with notes — a permanent, shareable marker of this version.
internals: A tag is a name that points at one commit and never moves, unlike a branch.
An annotated tag (`-a`) stores a message, author and date, so it carries release metadata.
A GitHub release is the tag plus human notes, listed on the Releases page and linkable from support tickets and changelogs.
Pushing the tag is a separate step from pushing commits — tags don't travel automatically.

keyCommands.note: Create an annotated tag on the current commit.
Publish a release from the command line.

commonMistakes: Forgetting to push the tag, so it exists only on your machine.
Tagging the wrong commit (check you're on the intended main).
Publishing a release with no notes — future-you won't remember what changed.
debrief.atWork: Every shipped version at a company is a tag and usually a release. It's how rollbacks, support and changelogs all refer to 'what exactly is running'.
debrief.interview: "What's the difference between a branch and a tag?" Answer: a branch moves as you commit; a tag is a fixed name for one commit, used to mark releases.
